strengths: The paper provides a rigorous and elegant theoretical unification of two previously disparate families of methods (noise-expectation and gradient-expectation) for training diffusion policies to target Boltzmann distributions, showing them to be special cases (η=0 and η=1) of a single reverse flow matching (RFM) framework. Appendix B carefully maps iDEM/DQS/QNE/RSM into this unified language, which is a valuable contribution to the field's conceptual clarity.

The reverse inferential perspective (treating the noisy sample as evidence and the endpoints as latent variables) is a clean and well-motivated reformulation of conditional flow matching that correctly reduces to a tractable posterior mean estimation problem; Proposition 1 and Theorem 1 establish the needed equivalences with careful, complete proofs.

The introduction of (generalized) Langevin Stein operators to build zero-mean, vector-valued control variates for posterior mean estimation is a genuinely novel technical device in this RL context, and the paper derives closed-form variance-minimizing coefficients (Propositions 4 and 5) under both general diagonal and isotropic parameterizations, giving a principled way to interpolate between Q-value and Q-gradient information.

The framework is shown to extend naturally beyond diffusion policies (Gaussian source) to general flow policies with arbitrary source distributions, and further to score-based models with non-Gaussian sources via the 'reverse score matching' extension in Appendix A, broadening applicability.

The RL instantiation (Section 4.4, Algorithm 1) is concretely specified with importance weights, SNIS-CV estimator, and practical numerical stabilization details (e.g., tmin cutoff), aiding reproducibility of the core method.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is thin relative to the theoretical scope of the paper: results are presented only as training-curve plots on 8 DMC tasks with no accompanying quantitative table of final/aggregate returns, no statistical significance testing, and no larger-scale or higher-dimensional benchmarks (e.g., humanoid, manipulation) to assess scalability.

The central claimed benefit of the Langevin Stein control variates — variance reduction leading to more stable/efficient training — is never directly measured; there is no ablation comparing the SNIS estimator with vs. without control variates, nor a comparison of the optimal (Proposition 4/5) coefficients against fixed η=0 or η=1 baselines using the identical codebase/policy class, so it remains unclear how much of the empirical improvement in Figure 1 stems from the flow-policy formulation versus the variance-reduction mechanism itself.

Computational cost is not analyzed: the method requires N Monte Carlo samples with Q-gradient evaluations (for the η-weighted estimator) at every actor update, which likely increases wall-clock cost substantially relative to baselines (especially QNE/SAC); no runtime or sample-efficiency-per-wall-clock comparison is provided.

The paper does not report how Λ/η is set in practice (fixed vs. estimated online via Proposition 4, and at what computational overhead), nor sensitivity to the number of SNIS samples N, both of which are important reproducibility and practical-cost details.

Baseline comparisons, while using diffusion-policy methods, do not include a flow-policy baseline outside the RFM framework (e.g., a naive flow-matching analogue of QNE/DQS without control variates) to cleanly isolate whether the observed gains arise mainly from moving to flow policies or from the proposed variance-reduction technique.

Some claims in the abstract/intro (e.g., 'improving training efficiency') are not directly substantiated with efficiency metrics (e.g., wall-clock time, sample complexity) beyond the qualitative training curves.
